page: The Vultr vhf-16c-58gb is an instance within the High Frequency Compute family, structured around a balanced hardware configuration. Built on an x86_64 architecture using shared Intel processors running at 2.0 GHz, the instance provides 16 virtual CPUs derived from 8 physical cores with 2 threads per core. Memory capacity totals 58 GB of RAM, yielding approximately 3.62 GB per vCPU. Storage is locally attached via a 1024 GB NVMe SSD, and the instance includes a complimentary public IPv4 address without discrete GPU acceleration hardware.

Benchmark outcomes show mid-tier general computing capabilities alongside noticeable constraints in memory throughput. CPU performance sits within the middle 50% across Geekbench (1548 single-core, 6764 multi-core), stress-ng (1884.79 single-core, 14058.95 multi-core), and PassMark CPU testing (12970.06). While cached memory access remains stable at 907.89 GB/sec for small 16 KB blocks, uncached large-block performance exhibits bottlenecks, falling into the bottom 25% for read bandwidth (24.85 GB/sec) and bottom 10% for write bandwidth (13.66 GB/sec).

Application and domain-specific benchmarks mirror this division in throughput. High-core tasks like software compilation via Clang (14012.0) and multi-threaded bzip3 decompression (66.17 GB/sec) perform solidly within median bands, while Redis achieves 11.03 million SET operations per second. Conversely, static web serving throughput measures at 6.08 GB/sec and PassMark physics evaluation settles in the bottom 25% percentile, reflecting the limitations imposed by shared-core CPU execution and uncached memory writes.

This hardware balance makes the vhf-16c-58gb practical for general enterprise application hosting, moderate database systems leveraging local NVMe storage, and CI/CD build environments. Workloads requiring sustained high uncached memory bandwidth, intensive numerical physics calculations, or hardware acceleration are less compatible with this configuration.
